On October 9, we presented our paper at COMPAS 2026, hosted by the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Dhaka.

Our paper is titled “A Low-Complexity Hierarchical NIDS for IIoT: Profiling Computational Overhead and Mitigating Data Leakage.”

Industrial IoT needs intrusion detection that runs at the edge, not in the cloud. But much of the published work reports inflated accuracy because random cross-validation leaks future information into training.

Our approach:
  • A two-stage hierarchical NIDS: fast triage first, deeper diagnosis only for flagged traffic
  • Strict chronological evaluation instead of random splits
  • Profiled computational overhead to set an upper-bound baseline for edge feasibility

Our key finding: random splitting inflated performance by up to 21 percentage points on DataSense (CICIIoT2025).

This is a single-dataset case study, so cross-dataset replication and embedded hardware validation come next.

A big thank you to my co-author Mir Suhail Asarat for their hard work on this, and to Md Samsuzzaman sir for the guidance. Thanks also to the COMPAS 2026 organizers and everyone who stopped by with questions and feedback.

#CyberSecurity #MachineLearning #IntrusionDetection #DataSense #CICIIoT2025 #NIDS #EdgeComputing #IIoT #COMPAS2026

Our paper "A Low-Complexity Hierarchical NIDS for IIoT: Evaluating Edge Feasibility and Mitigating Temporal Data Leakage" got accepted at IEEE COMPAS 2026, running October 9-10.

Co-authored with Mir Suhail Asarat.

Most IIoT intrusion detection papers report accuracy above 99%. We found out why: random cross-validation lets models train on future packets to predict past attacks. When we switched to a strict chronological split on the DataSense benchmark, the top models' Macro-F1 dropped sharply, purely from that leakage.

So we built a two-stage pipeline instead. Stage 1 is an XGBoost classifier plus network-layer heuristics that triages MQTT telemetry. Stage 2 only runs on flagged traffic: a DCNv2 model, small enough for a gateway with 1GB of RAM.

We also tested zero-day generalization by holding out each attack type during training. Recall stayed above 98% on Brute Force and MITM, but dropped to 26.70% on Malware, because MQTT telemetry alone can't see attacks that spread purely over the network layer. We reported that number instead of hiding it, since it marks exactly where this kind of detection stops working.

Thanks to Mir Suhail Asarat for the collaboration on this one.

#IIoT #NetworkSecurity #IntrusionDetection #EdgeComputing #MachineLearning

From a web server to full Active Directory Domain Admin...

It took me almost 4 hours to complete the Certified Red Team Analyst (CRTA) lab by Cyber Warfare Labs, and the multi-stage attack chain was an incredible learning experience. It simulated a realistic enterprise infrastructure spanning three network segments, requiring a complete shift from web application exploitation to advanced Active Directory forest abuse.

Here is a quick breakdown of the kill chain:
 • External foothold: Exploit command injection in a PHP newsletter form, read the /etc/passwd GECOS field, and recover a plaintext SSH password.  
 • Pivoting: Extract domain credentials from the Firefox database history and open a Ligolo-ng tunnel into the internal network segment.  
 • Lateral movement: Log into the management workstation to dump LSA Secrets and extract a plaintext service account password. 
 • Child domain compromise: Use a WMI shell on the child domain controller to run an offline ntdsutil IFM backup and retrieve the krbtgt AES-256 key.  
 • Forest dominance: Forge a cross-domain Kerberos ticket with injected Extra-SIDs to run a DCSync attack, extract the parent Administrator NTLM hash, and establish a PsExec SYSTEM shell.

Key Red Teaming Takeaways:
 • Browser History is a Goldmine.
 • Modern tunneling tools like Ligolo-ng make navigating deep, multi-segmented environments incredibly efficient.
 • Active Directory child domains must be treated as security boundaries; if a child domain falls, the parent domain is often only one forged Kerberos ticket away.

👇 Want to read the full, deep-dive technical breakdown, including the exact commands used, Nmap configurations, and the complete network diagram?

Imagine you apply for a job. The result comes back: “Rejected.” No explanation at all! Most ML models still work like this.

XAI helps you understand the “gossip” of a model. And depending on what kind of gossip you want to hear, you choose either SHAP or LIME.

For the job selection example, SHAP explains it by saying your experience is low, your skills don’t match, and there are some gaps in your profile that led to the rejection.

LIME works a bit differently here.

Let’s say the same job application is explained using LIME. LIME first takes your profile and creates many “fake but similar” profiles around it. Then it checks if we slightly increase experience or fix a skill mismatch, does the result change from “Rejected” to “Selected”? By testing these small changes, LIME figures out which factors are actually influencing the decision the most.

Basically, SHAP finds the culprits, while LIME shows what changes could potentially shift the outcome.

Why XAI is needed:
 • In cybersecurity, it helps explain why an activity is flagged as suspicious.
 • In healthcare, it helps justify risk predictions and detect bias or errors.
 • In finance, it helps explain loan or approval decisions and check whether the system is fair.

I recently completed the Explainable AI in Python course on DataCamp.
Many machine learning models are complicated, making it hard to see how they reach conclusions. This course focused on making those models transparent and easy to understand.

I learned how to use SHAP and LIME to break down model decisions. Global explainability shows which features affect the model as a whole. Local explainability tells you exactly why the model made a specific prediction for a single data point.

In fields like finance, healthcare and cybersecurity, accuracy is not enough. You have to explain the reasoning behind a decision to build trust and catch biases. This training helps me build machine learning tools that are both accurate and accountable.

I had previously applied XAI in my 7th semester thesis on Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS). After completing this mini course on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) Concepts, my understanding of transparency, interpretability, and accountable AI has deepened further.

Excited to keep building clearer and more trustworthy AI solutions.
#ExplainableAI #ArtificialIntelligence #DataScience #Cybersecurity #NIDS #ContinuousLearning

Sharing my experience of BrainStation23’s third-phase, day-long assessment for the Star Coder 2025 program.

Yesterday was the third phase of the Star Coder 2025 program by Brain Station 23. It was a day-long assessment held at their office in Mohakhali, Dhaka.

A total of 124 applicants (112 Software Engineer applicants and 12 SQA Engineer applicants) participated in this phase.

The reporting time was 8:30 am at the office. After a brief welcome session, we were given an overview of the assessments.

The first test consisted of two personality tests: one on Truity and the other on BrainStation23’s exam portal.

Following the first test, applicants were divided into groups of 6 through some fun games, with each group comprising 5 Software Engineer applicants and 1 SQA Engineer applicant. We were then given 6 tags—OwnPATH (team lead), Ownership, Passionate, Agility, Team Spirit, and Honesty—and were instructed to discuss within our team and assign the roles among ourselves over breakfast. I was honored to take on the OwnPATH (team lead) role in my team.

For the second test, each team was given 2 hours to design a system and solve some tasks on paper, which were then presented. The use of phones or the internet was not allowed. Two assessors (one from HR and another from the development team) assisted each team with clues and hints to solve the tasks and monitored team members on leadership, communication, teamwork, and passion.

Our team’s task was to design an E-Ticketing system. We were given 5 tasks to complete:
1. Requirement analysis
2. System architecture flow
3. Flowcharts for registration and login with specific constraints
4. Pseudocode for some tasks involving roles and permissions
5. Queries to retrieve specific data from the database we were to design.

After two hours, we had lunch and presented our solution to the assessors.

For the third test, applicants were evaluated on their selected stacks. We were given 20 minutes to answer questions related to our chosen language/stack.

For the fourth and final test, applicants had one-on-one interviews where questions were asked about the skills and projects mentioned in their resumes during the application process.

It was a fun experience! We played games, enjoyed coffee, and met many talented individuals. Overall, it was a memorable day for me.
